title: Colons, semicolons & dashes
examples: When should I use a colon instead of a comma?
Is it okay to use a dash in a sentence?
What is the difference between a semicolon and a colon?

explain.say: Today we are looking at three punctuation marks. They are the colon, the semicolon, and the dash. These help us join ideas in writing.

items: Dashes create sudden emphasis or breaks.

explain.say: We use a colon to introduce a list or an explanation. For example, I need three things: bread, milk, and eggs.

draw.text: Example: I need three things: bread, milk, and eggs.

explain.say: A semicolon connects two complete sentences that are closely related. For instance, the rain stopped; the sun came out.

draw.text: Example: The rain stopped; the sun came out.

explain.say: We use a dash to create a strong break or to add sudden emphasis. Try this: my favorite color—blue—is calming.
In real life you might see these when writing instructions. For example, first: preheat the oven; next: mix the dry ingredients.
A common mistake is using a comma where a semicolon is needed. Remember, a semicolon joins two full sentences, not just related ideas.

faq.q: When should I use a colon?
faq.a: Use a colon when you introduce a list or when you want to explain something that came before it. You can also use it after a complete sentence.
asks: Does a colon always mean a list?

faq.q: What is the difference between a semicolon and a colon?
faq.a: A colon introduces what follows, like a list. A semicolon joins two complete sentences that are closely related in meaning.
asks: Can I use a semicolon like a colon?

faq.q: When is it best to use a dash?
faq.a: Use a dash to create a dramatic pause or to add extra information that interrupts the main flow of thought. It gives a feeling of suddenness.

faq.q: Can I use all three marks in one paragraph?
faq.a: Yes, you can use all three marks depending on the relationship between your ideas. Think about what you want to emphasize in each spot.
asks: Do I need to know all three?

faq.q: Do I need a comma before a semicolon?
faq.a: Generally, you do not need a comma before a semicolon. The semicolon itself shows the strong pause needed.
asks: Is a comma always wrong before a semicolon?
What punctuation goes before a semicolon?

facts: A colon can follow a complete sentence to introduce a list or explanation.
A semicolon connects two independent clauses that are closely related.
A dash can set off an appositive phrase for sudden emphasis.
Do not use a colon if the text following it is not a list or explanation.

quiz.say: The team needed three things: players, coaches, and a strategy.
quiz.show: The team needed three things: players, coaches, and a strategy.

options.show: The team needed three things, players, coaches, and a strategy.
options.say: The team needed three things, players, coaches, and a strategy.

options.show: The team needed three things; players, coaches, and a strategy.
options.say: The team needed three things; players, coaches, and a strategy.

options.show: The team needed three things—players, coaches, and a strategy.
options.say: The team needed three things—players, coaches, and a strategy.

quiz.why: A colon correctly introduces the list of three things the team needed.

wrong.0: A comma is too weak to introduce a formal list like this.
wrong.1: A semicolon connects two full sentences, not a list introduction.
wrong.2: While dashes can set off phrases, a colon is standard for introducing a list.

quiz.say: The storm raged all night; the town remained safe.
quiz.show: The storm raged all night; the town remained safe.

options.show: The storm raged all night: the town remained safe.
options.say: The storm raged all night: the town remained safe.

options.show: The storm raged all night, the town remained safe.
options.say: The storm raged all night, the town remained safe.

options.show: The storm raged all night—the town remained safe.
options.say: The storm raged all night—the town remained safe.

quiz.why: The two parts are complete sentences that are closely related by the topic of the storm.

wrong.1: A colon suggests the second part explains the first, which is not the case here.
wrong.2: This comma splice incorrectly joins two full, related sentences.
wrong.3: A dash suggests a sudden break, but the connection is more of a balanced relationship.

quiz.say: My friend—the one who loves space—visited the museum.
quiz.show: My friend—the one who loves space—visited the museum.

options.show: My friend; the one who loves space; visited the museum.
options.say: My friend; the one who loves space; visited the museum.

options.show: My friend, the one who loves space, visited the museum.
options.say: My friend, the one who loves space, visited the museum.

options.show: My friend: the one who loves space: visited the museum.
options.say: My friend: the one who loves space: visited the museum.

quiz.why: The dashes effectively set off the extra description about the friend for emphasis.

wrong.0: Semicolons are used between full sentences, not inside a single clause.
wrong.2: Commas are fine for non-essential information, but dashes give stronger emphasis.
wrong.3: Colons are not used to interrupt a sentence like this.
